title: Simplifying and Rationalizing Radicals
short: Simplify roots and clear them from denominators.
trouble: Students multiply only the numerator by the conjugate.

blocks.html: You already simplify square roots like $\sqrt{72} = 6\sqrt{2}$ (Adding and Multiplying Radicals). The same idea works for any root, and one more skill finishes the job: clearing roots out of a denominator. It builds on nth Roots.

To simplify $\sqrt[n]{a}$, pull out the largest perfect $n$th power: $\sqrt[3]{54} = \sqrt[3]{27 \cdot 2} = 3\sqrt[3]{2}$. To rationalize $\frac{c}{\sqrt{b}}$, multiply top and bottom by $\sqrt{b}$. To rationalize $\frac{c}{a + \sqrt{b}}$, multiply top and bottom by the conjugate $a - \sqrt{b}$.

The product rule $\sqrt[n]{xy} = \sqrt[n]{x}\,\sqrt[n]{y}$ (for nonnegative $x$, $y$) lets you split off the perfect power, whose root is a whole number. Rationalizing multiplies by a form of 1, so the value stays the same. The conjugate works because of the difference of squares: $(a + \sqrt{b})(a - \sqrt{b}) = a^2 - b$, which has no root left.

blocks.title: A cube root
steps: The largest perfect cube factor of 40 is 8: $40 = 8 \cdot 5$.

blocks.html: Multiplying only the numerator by the conjugate (or by $\sqrt{b}$). That changes the value: you must multiply by $\frac{3 + \sqrt{5}}{3 + \sqrt{5}}$, which is 1. A quick check with a calculator: $\frac{4}{3 - \sqrt{5}} \approx 5.236$ and $3 + \sqrt{5} \approx 5.236$.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: $f(x) = \frac{4}{3 - \sqrt{x}}$ and the rationalized form $g(x) = \frac{4(3 + \sqrt{x})}{9 - x}$ are the same function (away from $x = 9$). At $x = 5$ both equal $3 + \sqrt{5}$.
